statement: A ladder 6.5 m long leans against a vertical wall, with its foot on level ground 1.6 m from the wall. The foot slides 1.7 m further away from the wall while the top stays against the wall. How far down the wall does the top slide?

choices.misconception: I assumed the top slides down exactly as far as the foot slides out, without drawing the two triangles.
I subtracted the new distance of the foot from the wall, 3.3 m, from the old height, 6.3 m, mixing up which side of the triangle is which.
I found the new height of the top, 5.6 m, and gave that instead of how far the top moved.
I found the original height of the top, 6.3 m, and stopped there.

hints: Draw the ladder twice: before the slide and after it.
Each position makes a right triangle with the ladder as the longest side. Find the height of the top in each picture with Pythagoras, then compare the two heights.
Work in decimetres to avoid decimals. Before the slide the height is the square root of (65 squared - 16 squared); after it the foot is 33 dm from the wall.

solutions.reliable: Work in decimetres: the ladder is 65 dm and the foot starts 16 dm from the wall. Before the slide the top is at the square root of (4225 - 256) = the square root of 3969 = 63 dm. After it the foot is 16 + 17 = 33 dm out, so the top is at the square root of (4225 - 1089) = the square root of 3136 = 56 dm. The top slides 63 - 56 = 7 dm, that is 0.7 m. The transferable idea: a quick sketch of each state turns a wordy motion problem into two familiar right triangles.
solutions.elegant: Both triangles come from Pythagorean triples with longest side 65: 16, 63, 65 and 33, 56, 65. The top falls 0.7 m while the foot moves 1.7 m, so the two ends clearly do not move by the same amount.

whyOnTest: Drawing both positions shows the top and the foot move by different amounts, which is the trap behind the most common wrong answer.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
